title: Misinformation or education? A comparative analysis of Instagram posts related to full mouth rehabilitation
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 144 Instagram posts retrieved from 12 full-mouth-rehabilitation hashtags. Each post was coded on a binary factual / non-factual scale against peer-reviewed literature, clinical guidelines and professional dental sources, and the paper reports 125/144 (86.8%) non-factual with the denominator stated. That is a share of items in a sample coded misleading or inaccurate, so CONTENT.

estimates.country: not stated (Instagram posts retrieved by hashtag; 75% English-language, 25% other languages)
estimates.date: not stated; collected on a single day, on or before 28 February 2025 (manuscript received)
estimates.measure_type: % of Instagram posts about full mouth rehabilitation coded as containing non-factual claims
estimates.denominator: 144 Instagram posts, the top 12 ranked posts for each of 12 full-mouth-rehabilitation hashtags, after removing irrelevant and duplicate posts
estimates.definition: post coded non-factual if its content did not align with peer-reviewed literature, clinical guidelines or professional dental sources; non-factual claims included misleading statements, exaggerated treatment outcomes, or incorrect procedural descriptions (examples given: 'permanent whitening with FMR', 'instant bite correction')
estimates.misinfo_def: "A post was classified as factual if its content aligned with peer-reviewed literature, clinical guidelines, or professional dental sources. Non-factual claims included misleading statements, exaggerated treatment outcomes, or incorrect procedural descriptions."
estimates.page_loc: Table 1 'Characteristics of posts under full mouth rehabilitation related hashtags (n = 144)', 'Accuracy of claims' row; repeated in the Abstract and in Results, 'Background characteristics of Instagram posts'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two trained researchers coded independently after a calibration pilot; weighted kappa 0.775 for inter-rater agreement and 0.820 and 0.720 for intra-rater agreement (re-coding of 50 posts one week later); conflicts resolved by a gold-standard examiner. The standard of truth is alignment with peer-reviewed literature, clinical guidelines or professional dental sources, not fact-checks.
estimates.moderator_quote: For each hashtag, the top 12 ranked posts were retrieved following Instagram's search and discovery algorithm. Posts deemed irrelevant or duplicate were excluded.
estimates.notes: borderline=true for a validity reason an adjudicator should weigh. The numerator definition is falsity-based (misleading statements, exaggerated outcomes, incorrect procedural descriptions), which is why this is coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY. But the same table reports that 56.9% of the 144 posts carry no written description at all, and 22 of 22 experience-sharing posts (100%) were coded non-factual. A wordless before-and-after marketing image cannot state a false claim, so the label appears to be capturing promotional framing and absence of clinical context as much as stated falsehood. The 86.8% should not be read as 86.8% of posts making a demonstrably false claim. Denominator is rank-truncated (top 12 per hashtag), hence denom_selection=curated. Collection date is not given; year coded 2025 from the 28 February 2025 receipt date.

missed_or_uncertain: Subgroup accuracy breakdowns over the same 144 posts were not given separate rows, to avoid double-counting: by theme (marketing 103/109 = 94.5% non-factual, experience sharing 22/22 = 100%, educational 0/13 = 0%; Table 2, p < 0.001), by account type (clinician 59/69 = 85.5%, dental interest group 28/30 = 93.3%, practice 38/45 = 84.4%; Table 3, p = 0.008) and by post type (clinical case 94/101 = 93.1%, procedure discussion 3/13 = 23.1%, practice advertisement 28/30 = 93.3%; Table 4, p < 0.001). Any of these could be substituted for the pooled row if the review prefers a stricter subset. Composition figures (75.7% marketing, 9% educational, 5.6% of posts by dentists, 59.0% watermarked) are not accuracy measures and were not extracted. The '29% of content could be inaccurate or misleading' figure in the Discussion is cited from another systematic review and is barred by R8. Two internal inconsistencies worth flagging: the Limitations say the study was 'restricted to English-language posts' while Table 1 reports 25% of posts in languages other than English; and Table 1's footnote reads 'except * n = 10' where the starred rows are n = 104.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Purposive hashtag frame: 12 FMR hashtags chosen for popularity, relevance and engagement; the top 12 algorithmically ranked posts per hashtag retrieved on a single day (date not reported) to control for Instagram's dynamic ranking, irrelevant and duplicate posts excluded, giving n = 144. Two trained coders worked independently after a 50-post calibration pilot; weighted kappa 0.775 inter-rater, 0.820 and 0.720 intra-rater; disagreements resolved by a gold-standard examiner. Analysis in SPSS 22 with Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square with Monte Carlo correction, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons, alpha 0.05. No sampling of users and no response rate (platform content study). Main weaknesses: rank-truncated single-day convenience frame of 144 posts, no reporting of what proportion of coded posts contained any verbal claim at all, and a truth standard defined as alignment with professional sources rather than adjudicated falsity.
rob.item6_quote: To assess the accuracy of claims, posts were evaluated using a binary classification scale (factual vs. non-factual). This was adapted from previous methodologies in health misinformation research (10). A post was classified as factual if its content aligned with peer-reviewed literature, clinical guidelines, or professional dental sources. Non-factual claims included misleading statements, exaggerated treatment outcomes, or incorrect procedural descriptions.
